name: Pattern 9: Scheduling and Logistics
title: Pattern 9: Scheduling and Logistics
answer: Pattern 9 is the use of optimization software for behind the scenes school logistics such as bus routes, master schedules, substitute placement, lunch forecasts, and heating and cooling. It matters because these problems have too many combinations for a person to test by hand, yet the resulting decisions affect real families and must be owned by a person. The Boston bus route example shows both the savings and the risk that a mathematically sound plan can fail if families are not brought along.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: This pattern covers the operational planning that most families never see. Optimization software can plan bus routes, build a master schedule, place substitute teachers, forecast how many lunches to prepare, and manage heating and cooling. These tasks involve too many combinations for a person to test by hand, which is where software helps. The problem it solves is the sheer complexity of scheduling and logistics, but the decisions that come out of it still affect real families. Because of that, a person has to own the decisions.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or district, the pattern shows up in the work behind bus routes, the master schedule, substitute coverage, lunch counts, and building temperature. The text does not break this pattern down by grade band, so the practice is described at the district and school operations level rather than for a particular classroom or age group. A good logistics project brings families in early, explains the tradeoffs, and gives a person the final say. The Boston example shows that changing bell times, bus stops, or lunch schedules can disrupt the routines families build their lives around. The text points to Chapter 19 for the operations side of the district in detail.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book's evidence for this pattern is the Boston example. The district used an optimization model to redesign its bus routes, saving about $5 million a year and taking 50 buses off the road (Bertsimas et al., 2019). The same work produced a plan to change school start times that would have saved more money and moved most high schools to later starts. That plan was dropped after strong opposition from families whose schedules would have changed (Bertsimas et al., 2022). The text does not give a separate evidence label for this pattern, so the Boston case stands as the stated evidence.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits of this pattern are not only technical. The math can be right and the plan can still fail, because families build their lives around bell times, bus stops, and lunch schedules. The Boston start time plan was dropped after strong opposition, which shows that savings and optimization do not settle the matter. A good logistics project brings families in early, explains the tradeoffs, and gives a person the final say. The decisions that come out of the software affect real families, so a person has to own them. The text leaves the final say with a person rather than the model.
